records.sourceFile: The impact of non-operative hip and core injuries on NFL athlete performance.pdf

paper.citation: Tramer JS, Jildeh TR, Castle JP, Buckley P, Nowak C, Okoroha KR. The Impact of Non-Operative Hip and Core Injuries on National Football League Athlete Performance. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: Retrospective study of NFL players with non-operatively managed hip or core injuries from 2010 to 2016, compared with matched uninjured controls. All injured players returned to play; defensive players played fewer games and had lower power ratings after injury, and two years after injury they played fewer games than controls. Offensive players showed no difference from controls in cumulative post-injury performance.
paper.tldr: NFL players returned to play after non-operatively managed hip and core injuries. Defensive players played fewer games than they did before injury and fewer than controls in the two years after injury, while cumulative career performance did not differ from matched controls.
paper.methods: Retrospective matched-control cohort. NFL players with a non-operative hip or core injury from 2010 to 2016 (41 offensive, 71 defensive) were matched 2:1 to uninjured players by age, position, performance and NFL experience. Games played and offensive or defensive power ratings were collected from public sources for the injury season and two seasons either side.
paper.findings: All injured players returned to play, with offensive and defensive players missing 4.0 and 3.1 games on average. Defensive players played fewer career games after versus before injury (37.4 vs 58.1, p < 0.01) and had lower power ratings (133.9 vs 219.8, p < 0.01), and two years after injury they played fewer games than controls (9.5 vs 10.9, p = 0.04), but cumulative post-injury games and power ratings did not differ from controls. The offensive skill-player power rating fell after injury (341.8 to 205.7, p = 0.03) while controls showed no change, with no significant difference between injured players and controls.
paper.limitations: Injury data come from public reports with no clinical detail, and the hip and core injury groups are broad. Power ratings exclude linemen and kickers, and the abstract and discussion state that offensive players played fewer games after core injury (versus hip injury and versus controls) without a matching result in the tables; the defensive power rating SD also differs between text and table (128.8 vs 128.5). The design has no randomisation and cannot show that the injury caused the changes.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can expect NFL players with non-operatively managed hip or core injuries to return to play, most within the same season, after missing about 3 to 4 games. Defensive players played slightly fewer games than matched controls over the next two seasons (9.5 vs 10.9), but cumulative post-injury games and power ratings did not differ from controls.
paper.athleteDev: The study suggests return to competition is likely after a non-operative hip or core injury, but it covers only NFL players and does not measure development, training or skill outcomes, so it cannot guide training progression.
paper.rtp: The study supports the expectation that players with non-operatively managed hip and core injuries return to play, with an average of 3.1 to 4.0 games missed. It cannot show that any specific rehabilitation protocol shortens return or restores performance, because treatment was not recorded.

records.sourceFile: The increasing medioclegal cost in the care of high-level athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Latario LD, Deter CJ, Deter AM, Baratz ME. The Increasing Medicolegal Cost in the Care of High-Level Athletes. Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery. 2024.
paper.abstract: A descriptive study of 88 lawsuits over the care of athletes from 1992 to 2023, drawn from a legal research database. Most decided cases (45 of 82) were won by defendants. Plaintiff indemnities totaled about 186.6 million USD in 2023 dollars, with football representing 49%, and professional and collegiate levels of play were associated with higher damages. Linear regression showed an increasing trend in inflation-adjusted awards over 30 years.
paper.tldr: Malpractice claims over athletes' care were more often decided for the defendant, but awards in professional and collegiate cases were larger and have risen over 30 years. This is a legal and financial signal, not evidence about athlete injury outcomes.
paper.methods: Westlaw Precision was searched for malpractice cases involving athletes' care using paired keyword terms, with filters applied for malpractice. Plaintiff and defendant demographics, case outcomes and damages were recorded, and indemnities were converted to 2023 dollars. Analysis used descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U tests for univariate comparisons and linear regression of award size by year.
paper.findings: Of 88 cases, 37 were decided for plaintiffs and 45 for defendants. Median damages were higher for professional and collegiate cases (2.83 vs 1.84 million USD, p=0.048), while football participation, plaintiff sex, defendant specialty, wrongful death and age group were not significantly associated with damages. Inflation-adjusted awards to plaintiffs showed an increasing trend over time (p=0.014).
paper.limitations: This is a retrospective database study, so it may miss cases or include incomplete entries. The abstract gives 1992 as the start year while the methods give 1993, outcomes were not reported for all cases, and the level-of-play comparison covers only 29 of the 37 plaintiff cases (11 vs 18). The subgroups are small, and the study cannot show why awards changed over time.
paper.practicalImplications: The findings show that claims involving professional and collegiate athletes carried larger awards, which supports awareness of liability risk when treating these athletes. The authors suggest added preoperative counseling and institutional discussion of waivers, but this study did not test whether those steps reduce claims or affect care.
paper.athleteDev: This study cannot inform training or performance programming. It describes legal claims over athlete care, not performance interventions or training outcomes.
paper.rtp: It cannot guide return-to-sport decisions, because it reports lawsuit outcomes rather than clearance criteria, reinjury, or athlete function. Staff should not use the award data as a measure of return-to-play risk.

records.sourceFile: The influence of exercise-induced fatigue on inter-limb asymmetries - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Heil J, Loffing F, Büsch D. The Influence of Exercise-Induced Fatigue on Inter-Limb Asymmetries: a Systematic Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2020;6:39.
paper.abstract: The review asked how exercise-induced fatigue affects inter-limb asymmetries in healthy people. Thirteen studies were included, using running, jumping, squatting, soccer, rowing and race walking as loads, and the results depended on the load, the task and the parameter measured. The authors could not draw a clear conclusion and call for more systematic research, including sport-specific tasks and tests before, after and during loading.
paper.tldr: Fatigue-related changes in limb asymmetry were inconsistent across 13 small studies, so the review cannot say whether fatigue raises the asymmetry that is linked to non-contact injury. Test asymmetry with sport-specific tasks before and after training, and do not rely on fixed asymmetry cut-offs.
paper.methods: A PRISMA-guided search of Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, SURF and SPONET in January 2020 identified studies of healthy people that calculated inter-limb asymmetry before and after, or during, a loading protocol. Study quality was rated with a 9-item, 18-point scale adapted from Bishop et al., and effect sizes were calculated post hoc where missing.
paper.findings: Thirteen studies (252 participants) were included. Results varied: for example, Bishop et al. found a large effect on jump height asymmetry during repeated sprints, but only between the last two sets and baseline, Bromley et al. found large effects of a soccer match on some SLCMJ measures, and most other comparisons were small or non-significant. The authors state that no explicit conclusion can be drawn about the effect of exercise-induced fatigue on asymmetries.
paper.limitations: Protocols, tasks, asymmetry equations and outcomes differed too much for pooling, and many studies gave incomplete results or no effect sizes. Most included studies had small samples (about 10 to 40), two studies included athletes with a past ACL rupture, and none included upper limbs or measured injury outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose asymmetry tests that reflect the sport's demands, such as single-leg countermovement jumps, and test before and after a session to see whether asymmetry changes in your own athletes. The authors recommend individual analysis, a control group and longitudinal data, and they state that group-level thresholds do not show who is at higher injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: Use sport-specific asymmetry tests before and after loading to track changes within each athlete, since the review cannot say which tasks or protocols will show fatigue-related asymmetry. Report the asymmetry equation used so results can be compared across sessions.
paper.rtp: The review does not support using fatigue-related asymmetry changes to decide return to play. The authors note that the common 10 to 15 percent asymmetry thresholds used for return-to-play decisions have been criticized as arbitrary, and that group means do not show an individual's injury risk.

records.sourceFile: The injury mechanism of Achilles tendon rupture in professional athletes - A video analysis study.pdf

paper.citation: Yüce A, Yerli M, Misir A. The Injury Mechanism of Achilles Tendon Rupture in Professional Athletes: A Video Analysis Study. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2024;114(3).
paper.abstract: The study used video analysis to describe how Achilles tendon ruptures occur in professional athletes and what body posture is present at the time of injury. Of 42 analyzed injuries, most occurred during take-off or acceleration, or during stopping and turning. At rupture, the ankle was in dorsiflexion, the body was bent forward, and the knee and hip were in extension. The authors suggest the findings can guide neuromuscular, proprioceptive and balance training to prevent rupture.
paper.tldr: In this series of 42 professional-athlete ruptures, most happened without contact during take-off, acceleration or stopping and turning, with the ankle dorsiflexed and the trunk flexed. These movements can guide prevention drills, but the sample is small and based on public videos.
paper.methods: A retrospective observational study identified 114 Achilles ruptures in professional athletes from 1970 to 2020 through internet searches. Of 48 videos accessed, 42 with adequate quality were analyzed by three reviewers who had not previously done video analysis and who scored each video blindly for contact, game activity and body position. Agreement was assessed with Fleiss kappa, and joint angles were not measured because the videos were not standardized.
paper.findings: Of the 42 athletes, 35 (83.3%) had noncontact injuries, and the most frequent game activities were take-off or acceleration (40.5%), stop or rotate (38.1%) and landing (16.7%). At rupture, the ankle was dorsiflexed in 71.4%, the trunk was flexed in 73.8%, and the hip and knee were extended in 61.9% and 54.8% of cases. Intraobserver agreement was above 0.864 and interobserver agreement above 0.815.
paper.limitations: Videos came from different platforms with different angles and quality, so joint angles could not be measured and only qualitative positions were recorded. Injury data came from public records that may not be complete or accurate, and the sample is small, almost all male, and led by basketball players (18 of 42). The abstract and discussion give 38.5% for stop or turn, while Table 2 gives 38.1% (16 of 42).
paper.practicalImplications: The common activities (take-off, acceleration, stopping and turning) and the posture at rupture (ankle dorsiflexed, trunk flexed, knee and hip extended) can guide which movements to include in neuromuscular, balance and proprioceptive training. The authors also suggest sport-specific conditioning and strengthening, but the study did not test whether these reduce rupture rates.
paper.athleteDev: The take-off, acceleration and stop-and-turn positions can guide sport-specific neuromuscular and balance drills, particularly for basketball players, who were 18 of the 42 cases. The study does not measure performance outcomes or show that these drills prevent ruptures.
paper.rtp: The study does not inform return to sport. It does not report rehabilitation methods, surgical treatment or return-to-play criteria, although it notes that many athletes fail to return to their previous level. Its findings may help choose movements for prevention work, but they cannot guide clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: The injury rate in NFL players was increased following cancellation of preseason games due to COVID-19.pdf

paper.citation: Baker HP, Pirkle S, Cahill M, Reddy M, Portney D, Athiviraham A. The Injury Rate in NFL Players was Increased Following Cancellation of Preseason Games due to COVID 19. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2021.
paper.abstract: A retrospective review of NFL players placed on the injury report during preseason and the first four regular-season weeks from 2016-2017 to 2020-2021. Of 3,025 injuries, 582 occurred in weeks 1 to 4 of the 2020-2021 regular season, and the injury rate in those weeks was significantly higher than in the same period of three recent past seasons. The authors conclude that injury rates rose after preseason games were cancelled because of COVID-19.
paper.tldr: Injury rates in weeks 1 to 4 of the 2020 NFL regular season were higher than in the same weeks of earlier seasons, after the preseason was cancelled. This public-record study cannot show cause, since it measured no conditioning or fatigue, so treat it as a signal rather than proof.
paper.methods: A retrospective review used publicly available weekly injury reports from NFL.com, ESPN, CBS Sports, Pro-Football-Reference and Bleacher Report, with each injury checked against a missed game; the 2017-2018 season was excluded because its records were incomplete. Rates were calculated per 1,000 athlete exposures using roster sizes of 90 (preseason games 1 to 3), 75 (preseason game 4) and 53 (regular season) players across 32 teams. Risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals compared 2020 weeks 1 to 4 with the same weeks of prior seasons, using t tests and chi-square tests.
paper.findings: Of 3,025 injuries over the study seasons, 582 occurred in weeks 1 to 4 of 2020 and 1,292 and 1,151 occurred in preseason and regular-season weeks 1 to 4 of earlier seasons. Regular-season rates in 2020 were 5.2, 5.9, 5.0 and 5.4 per 1,000 athlete exposures, compared with 2.8, 4.5, 3.3 and 3.6 in 2016 to 2019, with relative risks of 1.88, 1.31, 1.53 and 1.48 (P of 0.01 or lower). Knee (16%), hip or groin (11%) and ankle (10%) were the most common sites, and 71% of injuries were from player contact.
paper.limitations: The data come from public records that may omit or misreport injuries, and injury severity, diagnosis and clearance were not available. The study did not measure deconditioning or fatigue, did not follow the 2020 season to its end, and cannot separate the cancelled preseason from other pandemic-era changes. Table 2 gives a relative risk of 4.09 for preseason week 4, which does not match its own rates (5.4 vs 1.9 gives 2.84), and the Results percentages for preseason (53%) do not share the 3,025 total (1,292 is 43%).
paper.practicalImplications: A shortened or missing preseason may be followed by a higher early-season injury rate, which supports managing early-season workload closely. The authors suggest questionnaire-based fatigue and well-being monitoring to guide recovery and training, but this study did not test any monitoring tool or intervention.
paper.athleteDev: The finding is consistent with the idea that losing preseason preparation raises early-season injury risk, but it does not show that any specific conditioning or load progression would prevent this. The authors speculate that deconditioning and fatigue explain the rise, but the study measured neither and tested no training intervention.
paper.rtp: The study does not inform return to sport. It counts injuries and missed games for the early season but reports no injury severity, rehabilitation or clearance criteria, and games missed for 2020 were not available.

records.sourceFile: The mechanism of anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the National Football League - A systematic video review.pdf

paper.citation: Schick S, Cantrell CK, Young B, Mosher Z, Ewing M, Elphingstone JW, et al. The Mechanism of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in the National Football League: A Systematic Video Review. Cureus. 2023;15(1):e34291.
paper.abstract: Video footage of NFL players with ACL injuries from 2007 to 2016 was coded for movement, contact and joint position. Most injuries involved deceleration, contact, heel strike, shallow knee flexion and valgus collapse.
paper.tldr: Most NFL ACL injuries seen on public video happened during deceleration, often with contact and heel strike, at shallow knee flexion. Video cannot show the forces on the ligament, so these are patterns rather than proven causes.
paper.methods: NFL injured reserve lists (2007 to 2016) identified 429 ACL injuries, and publicly available videos were found for 53 through a systematic Google search. Three reviewers independently coded speed, maneuver, contact, foot strike, joint angles and collapse direction, with 96 percent agreement before reconciliation.
paper.findings: Deceleration was present in 32 of 53 injuries (60 percent) and 31 (58 percent) involved contact, 20 of them direct to the knee. Heel strike occurred in 32 (60 percent), knee flexion was 0 to 30 degrees in 33 (62 percent), and valgus collapse in 28 (53 percent). Defensive backs (14, 26 percent) and receivers or tight ends (12, 23 percent) were most often injured.
paper.limitations: Only 53 of 429 injuries (12 percent) had usable video, so the sample is selected. The videos were made for fan viewing, not for kinematic analysis, and camera focus on the ball may under-record linemen. The authors state that video alone cannot assess ligament forces, and the design has no causation analysis. The authors' conclusion calls heel strike 'a major kinematic risk factor', but with no uninjured comparison this is a descriptive frequency, not a tested risk factor.
paper.practicalImplications: Movement patterns seen in these injuries, namely brisk deceleration, contact in the lower body or upper body, and landing with heel strike at shallow knee flexion, can be used to choose drills for football-specific ACL prevention work. The paper does not test any prevention programme, so the drills themselves remain unproven in this population.
paper.athleteDev: Use these patterns to check whether football drills include brisk decelerations, cutting and contact in shallow knee positions, the situations linked to injury here. Use them to guide drill selection, not to set loads or targets.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes how injuries happened and does not report recovery, readiness or outcome data.

records.sourceFile: The mechanism of hamstring injuries - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Danielsson A, Horvath A, Senorski C, Alentorn-Geli E, Garrett WE, Cugat R, et al. The mechanism of hamstring injuries - a systematic review. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2020;21:641.
paper.abstract: A PRISMA systematic review of how hamstring injuries occur, searching PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library. Twenty-six studies were included and grouped by method, and the authors conclude that stretch-type injuries follow extensive hip flexion with an extended knee, and sprint injuries most likely occur in the late swing phase.
paper.tldr: Stretch-type hamstring injuries are linked to extensive hip flexion with a straight knee. For sprinting, the review points to eccentric strain in the late swing phase, but this rests mainly on estimates rather than recorded injuries.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library, searched on 21 February 2017 and updated to July 2019, for English-language original studies on hamstring injury mechanism. Two authors screened and extracted data in duplicate and rated quality with a modified Downs and Black checklist (maximum 20). Results were synthesised qualitatively by study method.
paper.findings: Three stretch-type studies (dancers and water skiers, 12 to 30 subjects each) all reported injury with extensive hip flexion and a hyperextended knee. Of 10 kinematic studies, seven reported the swing phase (late or terminal swing proposed as highest risk), two stance phase and one both phases. Of 10 kinematic-EMG studies, five reported swing phase, one stance phase, two both phases and two other tasks, and three strength studies in football players gave inconclusive results. Three studies recorded an actual injury in real time, and two of these concerned the same subject. The median quality score was 8 (range 7 to 14) of 20.
paper.limitations: The abstract reports 2,372 screened studies, while the Results report 2,841 screened after 1,423 duplicates were removed from 4,264 identified; the Results figure is used here. Table 2 lists 9 kinematic-EMG studies while the text describes 10. Most conclusions are estimates from uninjured participants, and the injury-recording evidence is limited to three case reports. Conditions varied, with some treadmill studies at slow speeds and no studies on grass, quality was low, and the inclusion criterion depended on the authors' own extrapolation.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat late-swing eccentric loading as a working hypothesis for sprint hamstring injury, and for kicking or dance-type movements check for the combination of hip flexion with a straight knee. The review does not test any prevention or training intervention, so it cannot show which exercises reduce injury.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review to frame hamstring risk in sprinters around late-swing eccentric load, and in kicking or dance around extensive hip flexion with a straight knee. It can guide exercise selection, but the mechanism evidence is largely estimated.
paper.rtp: The review describes how injuries happen, not how to rehabilitate them. The authors suggest that knowledge of forward trunk lean and hip and core control could inform prevention and rehabilitation programmes, but the review gives no return-to-sport criteria or timelines.

records.sourceFile: The prevalence and influence of new or worsened neck pain after a sport-related concussion in collegiate athletes - A study from the CARE Consortium.pdf

paper.citation: King JA, Nelson LD, Cheever K, et al. The Prevalence and Influence of New or Worsened Neck Pain After a Sport-Related Concussion in Collegiate Athletes: A Study From the CARE Consortium. Am J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: Prospective cohort of 2,163 collegiate athletes with concussion from the CARE Consortium. New or worsened neck pain was reported after 47.0% of injuries, associated with sex, altered mental status after injury, injury mechanism and what the athlete collided with. Neck pain was associated with longer symptom duration and time to normal academic performance, but not with the duration of the return-to-play protocol.
paper.tldr: About half of collegiate athletes with a concussion have new or worsened neck pain, and it goes with longer symptoms. The authors recommend a cervical spine examination for these athletes, but this study does not show that neck treatment speeds recovery.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of a prospective CARE Consortium cohort. Preseason baseline testing, then assessments at 6 and 24 to 48 hours, when symptom-free, and at return to unrestricted play. New or worsened neck pain was a rise of at least 1 point on the 0 to 6 SCAT3 scale. Stepwise multivariable logistic regression identified correlates; chi-square and Wilcoxon tests compared recovery outcomes.
paper.findings: New or worsened neck pain occurred in 1,016 of 2,163 athletes (47.0%). Associated factors in the final model included female sex (OR 1.48, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.89), altered mental status (OR 1.28), collision vs contact sports (OR 1.42), mechanism of injury, and striking the turf, ground, floor or ice. In the table, each extra hour of nightly baseline sleep was associated with lower odds (OR 0.94). Athletes with new neck pain had 11.1 vs 8.8 days of symptoms (P < 0.001), were less likely to resolve symptoms within 7 days, and took longer to return to normal academic performance. Return-to-play protocol length did not differ (P = 0.592).
paper.limitations: Observational design with no objective neck assessment to confirm a cervical injury. Severity data were missing for 267 athletes. New and worsened pain were not separated. Only NCAA and military-academy athletes were included, and neck pain was not measured in non-concussed athletes. The results text lists more baseline sleep as a factor linked to neck pain, while Table 3 shows lower odds per extra hour (OR 0.94); the table value is reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend a specific cervical spine examination for athletes with neck pain after a concussion and suggest considering early cervical intervention. They state that randomised trials are needed to show whether cervical interventions shorten recovery.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not address training or performance. It shows that concussed athletes with new or worsened neck pain stay symptomatic longer, so staff can expect a longer symptomatic period in that group.
paper.rtp: Neck pain after concussion was linked to longer symptoms and slower return to normal academic performance, but return-to-play protocol length was the same. The study cannot be used to set a faster or slower return-to-play timeline.

records.sourceFile: The prognostic value of MRI in     determing reinjury risk following acture hamstring injury - A systematic     review.pdf

paper.citation: van Heumen M, Tol JL, de Vos R-J, et al. The prognostic value of MRI in determining reinjury risk following acute hamstring injury: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2017.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of MRI findings at baseline or return to play as prognostic tools for hamstring re-injury. Eleven studies were included. No strong evidence was found for any MRI finding. Moderate evidence linked intratendinous injuries at baseline to re-injury, and a post hoc analysis of studies with sufficient sample size linked biceps femoris injury to re-injury.
paper.tldr: MRI findings at the time of injury or at return to play do not reliably predict hamstring re-injury. The strongest signals, intratendinous injury and biceps femoris involvement, come from few studies and should not drive return-to-play decisions on their own.
paper.methods: Systematic review registered with PROSPERO. Databases were searched without date limits to June 2016. Two reviewers screened studies and assessed risk of bias with a consensus-based tool. Data were not pooled because of heterogeneity; a best-evidence synthesis graded the evidence, and a post hoc analysis covered the two studies with at least 20 re-injuries.
paper.findings: Eleven prospective studies were included (seven low and four high risk of bias). At baseline, moderate evidence associated intratendinous injury and British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grade with re-injury, while Peetrons grading, the muscle involved, injury location, and length and cross-sectional area of the signal showed strong evidence of no association. At return to play, moderate evidence showed no association for fibrosis. The post hoc analysis of the two adequately powered studies reversed the muscle-involved result, showing moderate evidence of a moderate-to-strong association for biceps femoris involvement, and downgraded Peetrons grading to moderate evidence of no association.
paper.limitations: Most studies had few re-injuries (4 to 41), so type 2 error is likely. Re-injury was defined differently across studies and follow-up varied. Some studies counted symptom exacerbations as re-injuries. Only three studies adequately handled confounders. Only English, Dutch and German papers were included, publication bias is possible, and data extraction by one reviewer was suboptimal.
paper.practicalImplications: According to this review, MRI at return to play adds little for predicting re-injury. At the time of injury, the authors suggest MRI could be used to detect tendon involvement, which is hard to identify clinically, while biceps femoris involvement can be established by clinical examination.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not test training or load management. It suggests that hamstring injuries with intratendinous or biceps femoris involvement may carry higher re-injury risk, and it does not support using MRI at return to play to predict re-injury.
paper.rtp: This review addresses return to play directly. MRI findings at return to play showed no positive association with re-injury, so they should not be used alone to judge readiness. Intratendinous injury on baseline MRI may flag higher re-injury risk, but the evidence is moderate and limited by small studies.

records.sourceFile: The risk of all-cause injury and site-specific injury in athletes after concussion - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Liao M, Gu Y, Liu K. The risk of all-cause injury and site-specific injury in athletes after concussion: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025.
paper.abstract: Objective: to quantify the risk of subsequent all-cause, recurrent concussion, upper-extremity and lower-extremity injury after sport-related concussion. Methods: PRISMA-guided search of five databases for cohort studies through August 2025, scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and pooled with random-effects models, with subgroup and meta-regression analyses. Results: 19 cohort studies (86,879 athletes) showed higher odds of all-cause injury (OR 1.93), recurrent concussion (OR 3.06), upper-extremity injury (OR 1.76) and lower-extremity injury (OR 1.49). Risk was significant in studies with follow-up beyond six months and among college athletes, and sport type moderated the all-cause estimate. Conclusion: a concussion history raises later injury risk, and the authors argue for return-to-play protocols that include objective functional assessment.
paper.tldr: Across 19 cohort studies of more than 86,000 athletes, a prior concussion was associated with roughly twice the odds of a later injury and three times the odds of another concussion. Keep injury monitoring going for well beyond the first months after concussion, but the review does not show which return-to-play test would lower that risk.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO, searching PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science and EBSCO for English-language cohort studies. Included studies were scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (all 7 to 9 out of 9), adjusted odds ratios were preferred, and random-effects pooling used REML. Subgroup analyses covered country, follow-up duration, design, sport type and athlete level, with meta-regression and leave-one-out sensitivity checks.
paper.findings: Nineteen cohort studies (86,879 athletes) gave pooled ORs of 1.93 for all-cause injury (95% CI 1.39 to 2.68; I2 = 94.4%), 3.06 for recurrent concussion, 1.76 for upper-extremity injury (two studies) and 1.49 for lower-extremity injury (nine studies). The all-cause estimate was significant in studies with follow-up beyond six months (OR 1.94) and not within six months (OR 1.89, CI 0.91 to 3.94). Sport type was a significant meta-regression moderator (p = 0.038); athlete level and follow-up duration were not (p = 0.130 and p = 0.629). Egger's test gave p = 0.051.
paper.limitations: Most included studies are observational, five were unadjusted, and heterogeneity was very high, so the pooled estimates are averages across varied settings. The paper's claim that risk persists beyond six months rests on subgroup comparisons, since follow-up duration did not significantly moderate the effect, and the upper-extremity estimate is based on only two studies. The review also restricts to English-language papers and measures injury, not function, so it cannot confirm the authors' conclusion about residual deficits. The sport-type moderator came from a meta-regression with a precision interaction term, while the subgroup odds ratios themselves were nearly identical.
paper.practicalImplications: Flag athletes with a concussion history for injury monitoring; the largest pooled odds were for a further concussion (OR 3.06), with smaller elevations for upper-extremity (OR 1.76, two studies) and lower-extremity injury (OR 1.49). Keep surveillance going beyond the first six months, since pooled odds stayed elevated in longer follow-up studies.
paper.athleteDev: Use a concussion history as a reason to keep injury monitoring going through the season and beyond. Recurrent concussion carried the largest odds (OR 3.06); sport type was a significant meta-regression moderator (p = 0.038) even though the contact-only and mixed-sport subgroup estimates were similar (OR 1.94 and 1.90), so a single pooled figure should not be applied to every athlete.
paper.rtp: The review supports the idea that symptom resolution may not signal full readiness, because elevated injury odds appeared in studies with longer follow-up. It did not test any return-to-play tool or clearance rule, so it cannot say which objective assessment to use or when return is safe.

records.sourceFile: The role of genetic and  epigenetic factors in sports-related muscle, bone, and brain injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Marrouh A, El Haddouchi A, Kartti S, El Fahime E, Boutayeb S, Chagar Y, et al. The role of genetic and epigenetic factors in sports-related muscle, bone, and brain injuries. Science Progress. 2025;108(4):1-33.
paper.abstract: This narrative review explores how genetic variants (including ACE, ACTN3, AMPD1, VDR and APOE) and microRNAs (including miR-21, miR-133a, miR-208a and miR-214) relate to predisposition, severity and recovery in sports-related muscle, bone and brain injuries. MicroRNA levels are influenced by training and may serve as biomarkers. The review used targeted, nonsystematic searches of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science with no language or date restrictions, and grouped studies by injury type. Limitations include population heterogeneity, small samples and a lack of functional validation of the variants.
paper.tldr: This narrative review maps genetic and microRNA markers linked to muscle, bone and concussion injury in athletes. The associations conflict across studies and none is validated for screening, so the paper is best read as a research guide rather than a testing tool.
paper.methods: Nonsystematic narrative review. Targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO and Google Scholar used keywords on injury types, polymorphisms and microRNAs with athlete terms, with no language or date limits. Studies were selected for relevance and scientific value, supplemented by reference-list screening and citation tracking, and grouped by muscle, bone and concussion injury.
paper.findings: The review identifies 17 genes and 21 polymorphisms linked to muscle injury, 10 genes and 12 polymorphisms linked to bone injury, and six genes with eight polymorphisms linked to concussion. For ACTN3 R577X, several football studies associate the X allele with higher muscle injury risk, while six studies found no association. Circulating microRNAs such as miR-1, miR-133a and miR-208a rise after intense exercise, and salivary or serum panels distinguished concussed athletes in some cohorts.
paper.limitations: The nonsystematic search and absence of reported quality appraisal mean study selection may be biased. The authors note small samples, population and sport differences, conflicting results across studies, possible publication bias and population stratification, and the lack of functional validation for the variants. Some cited evidence comes from military conscripts, non-athletes or animal models, and the review does not pool effect sizes, so the strength of each association cannot be judged.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat these genetic and microRNA markers as research leads, not screening or selection tools. Do not use genotype to set training loads or return timelines for an individual athlete, since the associations are inconsistent and unvalidated.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest that markers such as ACTN3 or circulating miRNAs could in future guide training loads and recovery, but the review provides no evidence that this improves outcomes. Performance staff should treat genetic profiling as a future research question rather than a current tool.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest markers linked to slower tissue repair might justify more conservative return-to-play timelines, but none is validated for that use. The review cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport, including after concussion.

records.sourceFile: The role of virtual reality in the management of football injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Demeco A, Salerno A, Gusai M, Vignali B, Gramigna V, Palumbo A, et al. The Role of Virtual Reality in the Management of Football Injuries. Medicina. 2024;60:1000.
paper.abstract: The review summarizes virtual reality (VR) approaches for football injuries, covering prevention (biomechanical risk assessment, perceptual-cognitive training, heading), rehabilitation (low back pain, return to sport, kinesiophobia) and concussion education. It is framed around the high injury burden in football and the need for individualized prevention and rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: VR can recreate sport-specific movements and has shown early benefits for decision-making, heading, low back pain and fear of movement in small studies. Its effect on injury rates and return to play has not been established.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 10 February (year not stated), using lesion, rupture or injury terms combined with virtual, mixed or extended reality terms and soccer or football. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts and extracted data; a third resolved disagreements. Reference lists were also searched.
paper.findings: The review's tables list 14 studies, mostly single-session laboratory work with 2 to 60 participants. Reported results include VR training improving passing decisions and visual search in young players (Fortes et al., 2021), VR-trained players scoring more headed goals than controls over 10 days (Marshall et al., 2023), and VR reducing pain and kinesiophobia in players with chronic low back pain (Nambi et al.). A single-session VR concussion education study in children (Sullivan et al., 2024) found no significant change in attitudes toward reporting or reporting intentions.
paper.limitations: The authors state that standardized VR protocols are lacking and that randomized controlled trials are needed to test VR exercise efficacy and the reliability of VR movement analysis in sport. Most included studies are small, short and single-session, and the review does not pool results or appraise study quality.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports medicine and performance staff may consider VR as a supplement for perceptual-cognitive or biomechanical training and for low back pain or fear-of-movement work, where the evidence is preliminary. Its use for injury prevention or return-to-play decisions is not supported by the evidence reviewed.
paper.athleteDev: VR is a possible training aid for decision-making and heading skills in footballers, based on small studies with short follow-up. Coaches should not expect large or proven performance gains from it.
paper.rtp: VR may support post-injury rehabilitation for low back pain and kinesiophobia, and may be used to simulate sport-specific tasks during the late rehabilitation phase. The review does not establish VR as a return-to-play test, and clearance decisions should not rely on it.

records.sourceFile: The value of blood lactate and lactate clearance rate in evaluating the prognosis of athletes with heat illness of varying degrees after high-intensity exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Yu L, Dong X, Li H, Mi L. The value of blood lactate and lactate clearance rate in evaluating the prognosis of athletes with heat illness of varying degrees after high-intensity exercise. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2025;17:7.
paper.abstract: In a retrospective study of 36 athletes hospitalised with heat illness after high-intensity exercise, the authors compared blood lactate and lactate clearance between patients who recovered in under 7 days and those who took 7 days or more. Lactate was higher at admission, 2 h and 6 h in the slower-recovering group, and the 2-h clearance rate was an independent predictor of prognosis in logistic regression.
paper.tldr: In hospitalised athletes with heat illness, lactate that stayed high and a slow 2-hour lactate clearance went with a poor prognosis (7 days or more). The 45.5% clearance cut-off has not been validated outside this sample.
paper.methods: Retrospective observational study of 36 heat-illness patients admitted to an ICU in China (December 2019 to July 2024) after high-intensity exercise. Lactate was measured at admission, 2 h and 6 h, and lactate clearance rate was calculated against admission values. Patients were grouped by prognosis (under 7 days versus 7 days or more), and groups were compared with t-tests and chi-square tests, with Pearson correlation and binary logistic regression.
paper.findings: Lactate was lower in the good-prognosis group at admission, 2 h and 6 h (P < 0.05 or P < 0.01). At 2 h, lactate was 1.2 +/- 0.5 mmol/L versus 4.2 +/- 1.2 mmol/L, and at 6 h 0.8 +/- 0.3 versus 3.5 +/- 1.5 mmol/L. The 2-h clearance rate was higher in the good-prognosis group (P < 0.05). Admission lactate correlated with APACHE II score (r = 0.835, P < 0.01). Poor-prognosis rate was 22.2% with a 2-h clearance rate of 45.5% or more versus 55.6% below it (P < 0.05); the 6-h clearance rate was not significant.
paper.limitations: Retrospective single-centre design with 36 patients (14 poor-prognosis), and no external validation of the 45.5% threshold, whose derivation is not described. Eleven of the 14 poor-prognosis patients reached hospital more than 24 h after symptom onset, which the authors cite as a possible confounder. The abstract reports R2 = 0.83 for the LCR model, but the results give 0.835 as the correlation between lactate and APACHE II, and no model fit is reported for LCR. The text gives inconsistent study periods (December 2019 to July 2024 versus January 2020 to June 2024) and both a consent waiver and written consent, does not define what the 7-day prognosis cut-off measures, and has no exercise or performance data.
paper.practicalImplications: Heat-illness responses for high-intensity sessions could record lactate at admission, 2 h and 6 h, so that staff can see whether lactate is clearing. The 45.5% threshold should not be used as a decision rule until it has been validated in other samples.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure training, performance or adaptation, so it gives no basis for changing training prescription. Its relevance is limited to heat-illness response planning around high-intensity exercise.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its outcome is a 7-day prognosis split during hospital treatment, not return to play or competition.

records.sourceFile: The “Strengthen your ankle” program to prevent recurrent injuries- A randomized controlled trial aimed at long-term effectiveness.pdf

paper.citation: Van Reijen M, Vriend I, Zuidema V, van Mechelen W, Verhagen EA. The “Strengthen your ankle” program to prevent recurrent injuries: A randomized controlled trial aimed at long-term effectiveness. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017;20:549-554.
paper.abstract: In a 12-month randomised trial of 220 athletes with a recent ankle sprain, delivering the same neuromuscular training program by app or printed booklet produced similar rates of recurrent ankle sprains and similar improvement in ankle function scores. The authors conclude the two delivery methods are similarly effective when compliance is equal during the 8-week program.
paper.tldr: For athletes recovering from an ankle sprain, a free app and a printed booklet delivering the same 8-week program led to similar rates of recurrent sprain over a year. The result depends on compliance being equal, which the study did not measure over the follow-up.
paper.methods: Randomised controlled trial with 12-month follow-up in 220 athletes (18 to 70 years) recruited from October 2013 to April 2014, with recent ankle sprain as an inclusion criterion. Participants were randomised to the Strengthen your ankle app (n=110) or a printed booklet (n=110) with the same six exercises, three sessions per week for 8 weeks. Monthly online questionnaires collected sports exposure, self-reported recurrences and FADI scores. Incidence density per 1000 h was analysed with Cox regression, and FADI with Mann-Whitney U tests, on an intention-to-treat basis.
paper.findings: Self-reported recurrences were 70 in the app group and 69 in the booklet group (incidence density 15.59 vs 15.84 per 1000 h; HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.49). Injuries leading to time loss and to costs did not differ significantly. Median FADI rose from 92.9 to 100 in the app group and from 93.8 to 100 in the booklet group, with no significant between-group difference at any month. Cumulative recurrences per participant did not differ significantly between groups.
paper.limitations: Self-reported outcomes with no objective confirmation of sprains. Compliance was measured only during the 8-week intervention, and the authors assume equal compliance afterwards. The sample size was calculated from expected compliance rather than long-term injury rates, so power to detect long-term differences is limited. Table 2 gives a time-loss HR of 0.55 with a CI of 0.82 to 1.09, which does not contain its own estimate, so that row should be checked against the source. Participation in the trial may have influenced continued use of either method.
paper.practicalImplications: Either an app or a printed booklet can deliver this neuromuscular program, so the choice can follow local access and athlete preference. The study does not show that either format keeps athletes exercising for a year, so staff should still monitor adherence.
paper.athleteDev: The trial tests delivery methods for an injury-prevention program, not performance outcomes, so it offers no basis for changing performance training. Its relevance to athlete development is limited to how prevention exercises are delivered.
paper.rtp: Athletes in the trial were recruited within two months of a sprain, and the program was used as a preventive measure rather than a return-to-sport protocol. The study cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria, although the FADI results describe ongoing pain and disability after sprain.

records.sourceFile: Therapeutic peptides in orthopaedics - Applications, challenges, and future directions.pdf

paper.citation: Rahman OF, Lee SJ, Seeds WA. Therapeutic Peptides in Orthopaedics: Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions. Journal of the AAOS Global Research & Reviews. 2026;10(1):e25.00236.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarises the mechanisms, preclinical findings and safety and regulatory issues of therapeutic peptides used in orthopaedic injury and recovery. It concludes that clinical evidence is limited, that most peptides are not approved for orthopaedic use, and that claims should be framed as experimental.
paper.tldr: Peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 show healing effects in animal and mechanistic studies, but human trials are lacking. Most are not approved for orthopaedic use, and sourcing and anti-doping rules need checking before any use.
paper.methods: Narrative review by three physicians in sports medicine and orthopaedic practice. No search method, databases, date range or quality appraisal are described. The review groups peptides by function (wound healing, muscle and cartilage repair, sleep and recovery, neuroactive) and discusses mechanisms, safety, sourcing and regulatory status.
paper.findings: Most evidence is from animal models, mechanistic work and small prospective cohorts or case series. One case series of 17 patients reported reduced symptoms in more than 90% after intra-articular knee BPC-157 injections for tendon and ligament injuries at a minimum of 6 months. A meta-analysis of six RCTs is cited as showing that AOD-9604 did not change serum IGF-1. The review does not report any return-to-sport outcomes from clinical trials, and it notes wide variation in dosing and product quality.
paper.limitations: No stated search or appraisal methods, so the selection of evidence cannot be reproduced. Most cited evidence is animal or mechanistic, and the review does not grade it. Athletes are discussed mainly in terms of anti-doping rules and interest among wellness-focused groups, not as a studied population. Several statements, such as those on safety and on the power of cellular medicine, are asserted rather than tested in the cited evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff advising injured athletes on peptides should describe them as experimental, state that most are not approved for orthopaedic use, check the product source and its quality documentation, and confirm WADA status before any use by an athlete. Standard options listed in the review, such as physical therapy, NSAIDs, PRP, hyaluronic acid and surgery, remain the comparators to discuss.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not evaluate performance outcomes. It notes that several of the discussed peptides are banned for elite athletes because of possible performance-enhancing effects, so performance use should not be considered from this review.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It lists return to sport only as a suggested endpoint for future trials, and it reports no clinical return-to-sport data for any peptide.

records.sourceFile: Thoracolumbar fascia and lumbar muscle stiffness in athletes with a history of hamstring injury.pdf

paper.citation: Kellis E, Kekelekis A, Drakonaki EE. Thoracolumbar Fascia and Lumbar Muscle Stiffness in Athletes with a History of Hamstring Injury. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2024;23:436-444.
paper.abstract: Compared 11 soccer players with a previous hamstring strain and 13 uninjured players using shear-wave elastography of the thoracolumbar fascia and lumbar muscles. The injured group had greater fascia and paraspinal modulus and greater passive muscle activity in both passive and active tests.
paper.tldr: Soccer players with a past hamstring strain showed stiffer thoracolumbar fascia and spinal muscles than uninjured players in this small study. The result links lumbopelvic tissue to hamstring injury history but does not show that changing this tissue reduces re-injury.
paper.methods: Retrospective comparison of 11 players with a grade II biceps femoris long head strain in the past year and 13 uninjured amateur players. Shear-wave elastography measured the thoracolumbar fascia, erector spinae and multifidus during passive and active knee flexion at 0, 45 and 90 degrees and during prone trunk extension. Surface EMG and isometric knee flexion torque were also recorded.
paper.findings: The thoracolumbar fascia modulus was higher in the injured group in both passive and active tests. Erector spinae and multifidus modulus was also higher in the injured group. Passive EMG of these muscles was higher in the injured group, and knee flexion maximal torque was lower in the injured group.
paper.limitations: Small groups (11 and 13), a retrospective design and unrecorded rehabilitation. Probe orientation and position affect the stiffness values, and temperature was not controlled. The authors note their findings could reflect pre-existing differences rather than injury effects.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that management of players with a past hamstring strain could include interventions that alter lumbopelvic fascia and muscle stiffness. This study tested no intervention, so it does not show that such exercises change stiffness or reduce re-injury.
paper.athleteDev: The participants were adult amateur players with a past injury, so the study gives no evidence on how lumbopelvic tissue stiffness affects development or performance in younger athletes.
paper.rtp: The study does not measure return-to-play timelines or re-injury after any intervention. It can only suggest that spinal tissue be examined alongside the hamstring after injury, which has not been tested for outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Thursday Night Footballs impact on  all cause injuries in NFL players during 2012-2017.pdf

paper.citation: Baker HP, Lee KY-H, Dayton SR, Terry M, Tjong VK. Thursday Night Football's impact on all-cause injuries in NFL players during 2012-2017. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: Compared all-cause injury rates in NFL regular-season weekend games and Thursday Night Football games from 2012 to 2017, using weekly injury reports and injured reserve data. Thursday games had a slightly lower rate despite shorter recovery, and the authors conclude that dropping them is unlikely to lower injury rates.
paper.tldr: NFL Thursday night games, which give players about three days of rest, had a slightly lower all-cause injury rate than weekend games from 2012 to 2017. Injury reports cannot show whether injuries happened in practice or in games, so this is a short-term signal rather than proof that short rest is safe.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis. Weekly injury reports and injured reserve lists were collected for all 32 teams across five regular seasons. An injury was any reported injury not previously on a report. Rates per 1,000 athletic exposures, where one game equals one exposure, were compared using relative risk with 95% confidence intervals.
paper.findings: There were 9,621 all-cause injuries overall: 9,202 during weekend games (rate 7,598 per 1,000 exposures) and 419 during Thursday games (rate 6,072 per 1,000 exposures). The relative risk was 0.97 (95% CI 0.95 to 0.98), which the authors describe as statistically significant.
paper.limitations: The authors assumed injuries on the reports happened in games, which cannot be verified, and reports lack injury type, severity and time lost. The reported relative risk of 0.97 does not match the rates in Table 1 (6,072 vs 7,598 per 1,000 exposures, a ratio of about 0.80), the Discussion calls it a 3% absolute risk reduction, and weekend injuries are given as 9,202 in the text but 9,201 in the table.
paper.practicalImplications: These data do not support the view that Thursday games raise all-cause injury counts. They cannot rule out effects on injury severity, time lost or practice injuries, so they should not be used alone to judge whether three days of rest is enough.
paper.athleteDev: The study covers professional NFL players only, so it says nothing about how short recovery affects injury or development in younger players.
paper.rtp: The study does not report time lost, return to play or re-injury, so it cannot show whether short recovery between games affects how quickly players return. It counts new injuries only and says nothing about return timing.

records.sourceFile: Time of Season and Game Segment Is  Not Related to Likelihood of Lower-Limb Injuries- A Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Doyle TLA, Schilaty ND, Webster KE, Hewett TE. Time of Season and Game Segment Is Not Related to Likelihood of Lower-Limb Injuries: A Meta-Analysis. Clin J Sport Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: Meta-analysis of 15 studies (21 data sets) reporting ACL, groin and hamstring injuries in level 1 sports, with searches up to November 2017. Pooled odds ratios compared the first and second half of the season and of the game.
paper.tldr: Across the pooled studies, ACL, groin and hamstring injuries did not cluster in either half of the season or the game. Injury timing alone does not point to a window for prevention work.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided meta-analysis of PubMed, MEDLINE, SportDiscus, CINAHL and AusSport plus manual searches, with two reviewers screening and extracting data. Figure data were digitised where needed, risk of bias was assessed with the NHLBI observational cohort tool, and random-effects odds ratios were pooled.
paper.findings: First versus second half of the season showed no difference for ACL (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.78), groin (OR 1.79, 0.63 to 5.06) or hamstring (OR 1.16, 0.88 to 1.53) injuries. Between halves of the game there was no difference for hamstring injuries (OR 0.85, 0.58 to 1.24), and no clear difference for ACL injuries (OR 0.43, with a confidence interval reported inconsistently). Individual studies were mixed, especially for hamstring injuries.
paper.limitations: Few ACL data sets and one groin game study make the pooled estimates imprecise. Counts were not normalised to exposure, fatigue was not measured, and many studies lacked timing detail; the ACL game-half interval conflicts between the text (0.07 to 2.56) and the abstract and Table 4 (0.47 to 7.92), which should be checked before citing.
paper.practicalImplications: Injuries do not show a consistent seasonal or in-game pattern across these sports, so prevention work should not be scheduled around an assumed fatigue peak on this evidence alone. Future studies should report injury timing and exposure so they can be pooled.
paper.athleteDev: Does not support scheduling injury-prevention or load management around a fixed point in the season or game. Injury timing counts are not a measure of fatigue, so training decisions should rest on monitoring data.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the paper addresses when injuries occur, not when athletes return to sport or which criteria to use.

records.sourceFile: Timing of anterior cruciate ligament surgery.pdf

paper.citation: Zsidai B, Kaarre J, Narup E, Samuelsson K. Timing of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Surgery. Clin Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of ACL reconstruction timing. It covers how early and delayed surgery are defined and compares arthrofibrosis, clinical and functional outcomes, revision surgery, secondary meniscus and cartilage injury, and concurrent procedures.
paper.tldr: Early ACL reconstruction, within weeks to a few months of injury, appears at least as good as delayed surgery for function and return to activity, and may reduce meniscus and cartilage damage. The best cut-off between early and delayed surgery is still unclear.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search method. It discusses cited meta-analyses, registry analyses, cohort studies and randomised trials, and reviews definitions of early and delayed surgery and the role of concurrent procedures.
paper.findings: Cited studies define early surgery anywhere from days to months, which makes comparison hard. One randomised trial comparing surgery within 8 days with surgery at 6 to 10 weeks found no range-of-motion deficit at 6 or 24 months. Revision findings conflict across registries, and delayed surgery was linked to more medial meniscus injury (2.24-fold odds beyond 3 months in one meta-analysis) and more cartilage injury in cited studies.
paper.limitations: Narrative design with no described search or risk-of-bias method, so selection of evidence is not transparent. Causal effects of timing are hard to isolate because baseline MRI is not available, and many cited populations are general ACL patients rather than athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: The review suggests early reconstruction may be preferred when meniscus repair or extra-articular stability surgery is planned, because delay is linked to more meniscal and cartilage damage. Surgeons and researchers should define early and delayed surgery explicitly when reporting outcomes, since current definitions vary widely.
paper.athleteDev: The review says delayed surgery risks quadriceps atrophy and secondary joint damage, which matter most for athletes aiming for a fast return. Use this in the surgical timing discussion rather than to set training loads.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport planning because one cited trial found many patients reached Tegner 6 or higher after either early or delayed reconstruction. The review does not set a return-to-sport timeframe or test criteria.

records.sourceFile: Timing return to competition - A prospective registration of 45 different types of severe injuries in Germany's highest soccer league.pdf

paper.citation: Krutsch W, Memmel C, Alt V, Krutsch V, Tröß T, aus der Fünten K, et al. Timing return-to-competition: a prospective registration of 45 different types of severe injuries in Germany's highest football league. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg. 2021.
paper.abstract: Prospective media-based registration of severe injuries (absence over 28 days) in the first German professional football league across four seasons, 2014-15 to 2017-18. It reports injury frequency by body region and season, and return-to-competition times for 45 specific injury types.
paper.tldr: Knee injuries were the most common severe injury, and ACL ruptures had the longest median time to return to competition, about 222 days. ACL ruptures tended to occur early in the season, while muscle injuries peaked late.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort study using media-based registration from a sports magazine, social media and a transfer website, with each injury confirmed by at least one other source. Injury classification followed the Fuller 2006 consensus. Return-to-competition was measured from injury to the first official match reported in public media, and incidence was expressed per 1000 football hours using estimated training exposure.
paper.findings: Across four seasons there were 660 severe injuries (mean 9.2 per team per season; incidence 0.77 per 1000 hours). The knee was most affected (30.0%), followed by the thigh (26.4%) and ankle (16.7%). The 24 ACL ruptures had a median return-to-competition time of 221.5 days in Table 5, and ACL ruptures peaked in August to September (45.8%). Thigh muscle tears were the most frequent specific injury (n = 109, median 41 days).
paper.limitations: Media-based data without medical records, estimated training exposure, and return dates taken from the first reported match. The 109 injuries without a specific diagnosis were excluded, and several injury types have very few cases, giving wide spreads (for example, knee cartilage damage, SD 153 days). The 222-day ACL median in the abstract differs slightly from the 221.5 in Table 5.
paper.practicalImplications: The return-time benchmarks give typical time-loss by injury type for professional soccer and can help set expectations, while the seasonal patterns can inform when preventive work is timed. The data do not define clinical readiness, so they should not replace criteria-based return decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Shows that ACL ruptures cluster at the start of the season and muscle and ankle injuries toward the end, which may help decide when to focus preventive work. It gives no information on training prescription or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Gives typical times from injury to first official match for 45 injury types in one professional league, such as a median of about 222 days for ACL rupture. These are media-reported returns rather than criteria-based clearance, so they can set expectations but cannot fix an individual's return date.

records.sourceFile: Tired of ACL Injures - A Review of Methods and Outcomes of Neuromuscular Fatigue as a Risk Factor for ACL Injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Taylor JLI, Burkhart TA. Tired of ACL Injures: A Review of Methods and Outcomes of Neuromuscular Fatigue as a Risk Factor for ACL Injuries. Biomechanics. 2025;5:11.
paper.abstract: Structured review of lower-limb neuromuscular fatigue as an ACL injury risk factor, covering 67 studies and 1440 healthy young adults. Studies were included if they compared fatigued and non-fatigued states and measured at least one biomechanical variable linked to ACL injury.
paper.tldr: Localised leg-muscle fatigue changed biomechanics in a way linked to ACL injury risk in most studies, so it looks like one modifiable risk factor among several. Fatigue protocols and measures vary so much that there is no consensus on how to test it.
paper.methods: Structured Medline search run on 23 June 2023, with two-stage screening and data extraction. Included studies used healthy participants aged 18 to 35 and compared fatigued with non-fatigued states on at least one lower-limb biomechanical variable. Outcomes were coded as kinematic, kinetic, neuromuscular or proprioceptive and classed as increasing or decreasing ACL risk. No pooled meta-analysis was run.
paper.findings: Of 67 studies, 53 (79%) reported post-fatigue changes indicating higher ACL injury risk, such as reduced knee flexion, increased knee abduction or internal rotation, and increased anterior tibial translation. Fatigue protocols and end-points were highly variable, including volitional failure, RPE thresholds and fixed-time or cycle criteria. Only one study objectively measured neuromuscular fatigue, using EMG mean power frequency.
paper.limitations: Methods report 60 articles for extraction while Results report 67, so the sample size is unclear. There is no pooled estimate or formal risk-of-bias rating, most protocols did not measure fatigue objectively, and the included participants were healthy young adults, many of them physically active rather than athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Assessing movement in a fatigued state, and training controlled landing and cutting while tired, may be useful within ACL injury-risk programmes. The authors also suggest neuromuscular endurance work, which the included studies did not test.
paper.athleteDev: Supports checking landing and cutting quality after sport-specific fatigue as part of ACL injury-risk work. The fatigue protocols are not standardised, so no single protocol should be treated as validated for an individual athlete.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport testing because the authors suggest assessing movement in a fatigued state, but the review excluded participants after ACL reconstruction and so does not show outcomes after surgery or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Topical cannabidiol is well tolerated in individuals with a history of elite physical performance and chronic lower extremity pain.pdf

paper.citation: Hall N, James B, Bhuiyan MAN, Crane E, Falgout C, Murnane KS. Topical cannabidiol is well tolerated in individuals with a history of elite physical performance and chronic lower extremity pain. Journal of Cannabis Research. 2023;5:11.
paper.abstract: Open-label pilot with retrospective analysis of deidentified data from 20 former professional athletes with chronic lower-extremity pain after injury. Topical CBD (10 mg twice daily) was used for six weeks. Seventy percent completed the study, and half of completers reported minor adverse effects, none needing medical care. Self-reported pain fell significantly from intake to exit, and pain-related disability improved across all seven domains assessed.
paper.tldr: In former professional athletes with chronic lower-leg pain, topical CBD was generally well tolerated, with minor skin side effects in half of completers. Pain and disability scores improved, but without a control group those changes cannot be attributed to the CBD.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of deidentified data from an open-label pilot run by a private research group. Participants applied a topical CBD cream through a controlled dispenser (10 mg twice daily) for six weeks, after stopping other pain treatments including opioids, NSAIDs and acetaminophen. Outcomes were adverse events, the Pain Disability Index at intake and exit, the Lower Extremity Functional Scale at intake, and a daily pain journal, analysed with paired t-tests, correlation and regression.
paper.findings: Of 14 completers, seven (50%) reported adverse events, mainly skin dryness (43%) and rash (21%), which resolved without intervention; one man reported cold sweats and another a racing heart. Mean self-reported pain fell from 3.5 at intake to 1.7 at exit (P < 0.001). Pain Disability Index scores fell significantly in all seven activity domains (P < 0.001).
paper.limitations: A single-arm open-label pilot with 20 enrolled, 14 completers (six dropped by day 4 for unspecified reasons and were excluded), no placebo group and self-reported outcomes only, so the improvement cannot be attributed to CBD. The discussion reports 30% with adverse effects, but the results report 7 of 14 completers (50%), and the data-collecting organization is a for-profit entity wholly owned by one author.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff treating former athletes with chronic lower-leg pain should know that topical CBD was tolerated in this small pilot, with mostly mild skin side effects. The paper does not support recommending it for pain control; a randomized controlled trial would be needed before any change to care.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Not applicable. The participants were retired athletes with chronic pain, and the study measured no performance outcome.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Cannot inform return to sport. The study measured daily-function and pain scores, not sport return, re-injury or performance, so it should not guide clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Training load and injury - Causal pathways and future directions.pdf

paper.citation: Kalkhoven JT, Watsford ML, Coutts AJ, Edwards WB, Impellizzeri FM. Training Load and Injury: Causal Pathways and Future Directions. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Examines how specific training load measures and metrics relate to the causal pathways of gradual-onset and traumatic injury, through mechanical and psycho-physiological load-response pathways. Uses the acute:chronic workload ratio as a case study of a metric with weak conceptual foundations.
paper.tldr: Most training load measures sit too far from tissue damage to predict injury reliably. Use them mainly to check that athletes complete what is prescribed, not to judge injury risk.
paper.methods: Narrative review and conceptual analysis. No systematic search or new data are described; the ACWR is examined as a case study.
paper.findings: The authors state that a clear causal link between training load and injury has not been established. They conclude that common external and internal load measures poorly reflect tissue-level mechanical loading, and that the ACWR has conceptual flaws, including interchangeable inputs and a chronic load used as a proxy for resilience. They note that ACWR-injury associations have been reported in contradictory directions or not at all.
paper.limitations: No search or appraisal of the included studies is described, so selection bias cannot be judged. The critique is largely conceptual and does not quantify how far the evidence base is affected.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat training load metrics as tools for monitoring prescribed workload, not as injury-risk predictors. Do not change training to reduce injury risk on the basis of ACWR thresholds without a clear causal rationale.
paper.athleteDev: Use load data to confirm athletes complete the prescribed work and to guide periodization. Do not use the ACWR or similar ratios as the basis for changing an athlete's training, because the paper finds their conceptual basis weak.
paper.rtp: The review does not evaluate return-to-sport decisions and cannot be used to set return-to-play loads or to clear an athlete on the basis of an ACWR.

paper.citation: Carey DL, Blanch P, Ong KL, Crossley KM, Crow J, Morris ME. Training loads and injury risk in Australian football: differing acute:chronic workload ratios influence match injury risk. Br J Sports Med. 2016.
paper.abstract: Tests whether daily acute:chronic workload ratios explain non-contact injury risk in Australian football, and which workload variable and time windows explain it best. Uses 53 players over two seasons from one professional club.
paper.tldr: In this one-club study, a 3-day acute to 21-day chronic moderate-speed running ratio best tracked match injury risk. Ratios outside 0.8 to 1.2 carried about 2.4 times the relative risk, so test which windows fit your own schedule before relying on them.
paper.methods: Cohort analysis of GPS, accelerometer and session-RPE workload from 53 players over two seasons, with time-loss non-contact injuries recorded by club medical staff. Daily acute:chronic ratios for six workload variables and 56 window pairs were modelled against injury using quadratic regression on quantile bins.
paper.findings: Moderate-speed running (18 to 24 km/h) with a 3-day acute and 21-day chronic window gave the best model fit in matches (mean R2 0.79). Matches carried higher injury likelihood than training sessions (RR 4.04, 95% CI 2.86 to 5.70), and for the best model, ratios outside 0.8 to 1.2 had RR 2.43 (1.11 to 5.32). Acute window size strongly affected model performance, while a forward injury lag did not significantly improve fit.
paper.limitations: Data come from one professional club over two seasons, with 178 time-loss non-contact injuries in total but only 59 recorded in matches, and the match analyses also excluded precompetition and rehabilitation injuries. Other risk factors such as age and experience were not modelled, the best combination was chosen from 336 options, and R2 describes a fit to binned group means rather than individual predictions.
paper.practicalImplications: Track daily ratios using the workload variable and windows that fit your own competition and training schedule, rather than a default 7-to-28-day ratio. Read ratios outside 0.8 to 1.2 as a prompt to review the load, not as proof of cause.
paper.athleteDev: For Australian football, moderate-speed running load (18 to 24 km/h) was the best of the six workload variables tested, and the 7:28 distance ratio explained less. Set the acute window to match the schedule, using 3 days where a main training session falls between matches, and review sessions that push an athlete outside the 0.8 to 1.2 ratio range.
paper.rtp: The study covers time-loss non-contact injuries and does not test return-to-play loading. Players in rehabilitation were included in ratio calculations, but observations with chronic loads more than 2 SD below the mean (such as players returning from injury) were removed and injuries during rehabilitation were excluded from match analyses, so the paper cannot be used to set return-to-competition workloads.
